antyāvasāyin
(‘decided as the last’)
------------------------------------------
Apart from the four varṇas or groups of people in the society, a very large number of jātis or castes which have come into being as a result of mixing up of these varṇas, have been mentioned in the Hindu religious works. The names of most of these castes actually indicate their vocations and often, the status of the caste group depended upon the type of profession followed by it.
The groups considered almost as outside the pale of the चस्ते स्य्स्तेम् were called ‘antyajas’ (‘the least-born) and those considered as the last even among them were named ‘antyāvasāyins,’ for instance, caṇḍālas and śvapacas (eaters of dog’s flesh). They were considered as untouchables even among the untouchables and used to live in cemeteries. They were disqualified from appearing as witnesses in legal disputes.

antardhānatva
(‘the capacity to become invisible’)
------------------------------------------
Patañjali, the great teacher of योग, has described in his Yogasūtras several सिद्धिस् or miraculous powers, which a योगि can obtain through सṁयम. The practice of धारणा (fixing the मिन्द् on the object of meditation) and ध्यान (continuous flow of the mind—stuff towards it) ending in समाधि (superconscious experience) is called सṁयम.
When the योगि practises सṁयम upon the inherent capacity of his own body to be seen by others, thus controlling it, and by arresting its function, he becomes invisible to others. This siddhi is called अन्तर्धानत्व. See Yogasūtras 3.21.

antarvedi
(‘inside the sacrificial altar’)
------------------------------------------
The tract of land between the rivers गङ्गा and यमुना, stretching from प्रयाग (modern Allahabad) to Hardvār (or Hardwar) has often been called by this name. It has been regarded as a sacred region and the principal seat of ‘Ārya-ब्राह्मणस्,’ ब्राह्मणस् who were ideal in character and fit to be emulated by others. It has also been called ‘samasthalī,’ ‘śaśasthalī and ‘brahmāvarta.’
‘Antarvedi’ is also the name of a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे situated on the bank of the river गोदावरी.

antarikṣa
(‘that which contains स्तर्स्,’ the sky)
------------------------------------------
The region pervading the space in between the earth (bhūloka) and the heavens, (dyuloka or स्वर्ग), is called अन्तरिक्ष. It is also known as भुवर्लोक. According to the Ṛgveda, इन्द्र or वायु is the presiding deity of this region. Sometimes a few more deities are assigned to this region: Apām Napāt, Aja-ekapāt, रुद्र, Maruts, Parjanya and Āpaḥ (waters).

antardhauti
(‘internal cleansing’)
------------------------------------------
The science of हठयोग prescribes ‘dhauti’ or cleansing of the body to make it pure, healthy and strong so that it can withstand the rigours of राजयोग. This is one of the several techniques and is of four kinds: अन्तर्धौति, दन्तधौति, हृद्-धौति and मूलशोधन.
Antardhauti, the first of these, is again of four kinds: vātasāra, वारिसार, vahnisāra or अग्निसार and bahiṣkṛti.
In vātasāra, the purification is effec-ted by inhaling air (vāta = air) by shaping the lips like the beak of a crow, filling up the stomach with it and expelling it through eructation.
In वारिसार, warm saline water (vāri = water) is drunk and expelled through the rectum. This is later on followed by vamana-धौति, drinking saline water and vomitting it.
In vahnisāra, navel knot is pressed against the spinal cord by exhalation and contraction of the muscles of the stomach.
Bahiṣkṛti is similar to vātasāra except that the air is expelled through the rectum instead of through the mouth.
These techniques not only purify the body but also free it from diseases. However, they should be practised only under the personal guidance of an expert haṭhayogi.
See Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā 1.14-22 for details.

antyeṣṭi
(‘the last sacrifice’)
------------------------------------------
According to the धर्मशास्त्रस्, a Hindu is expected to lead his life reli-giously. At every stage of his life he is expected to perform or undergo certain religious ceremonies which will add a peculiar excellence not only to his body but also to his मिन्द् and spirit. This is technically called ‘saṁskāra’ (purificatory rite or sacrament). Out of the sixteen such सṁस्कारस् (called षोडश-सṁस्कारस्) अन्त्येष्टि is the one that comes at the very end. It is the grand finale of a life that has been well-lived.
As the very name indicates (antya = end, death) it is performed on the death of a person, by his survivors, usually the sons or the nearest male relatives. Since च्रेमतिओन् seems to have been the general rule among the Vedic आर्यन्स्, it was considered as a sacrifice (iṣṭi = sacrifice). It was believed that अग्नि, the fire-god, who acted as a messenger between gods and men, would lead the सोउल् of the dead to the next world.
On the approach of death, the person who is expecting to die shortly, bids farewell to the assembled relatives and the world. Alms and gifts are distributed. Oblations are offered into the sacrificial fire maintained by him. In the modern days dropping the water of गङ्गा and तुलसी leaves into his mouth are in vogue. The body is removed in a bier specially prepared and taken in a procession to the च्रेमतिओन् ground, being led by the chief mourner (usually the eldest son). A cow is let free on this occasion. She is called ‘anustaraṇī’ and is believed to be helpful in crossing the ocean of mortality. The corpse after washing is laid on the pyre and fire is applied with appropriate Vedic mantras (like Ṛgveda Saṁhitā 10.16.1). After udakakarma (offering of water) and consoling the mourners, the nearest relatives observe अशौच (ceremonial impurity) usually for three days. Later on, the bones are gathered (asthisañcayana) and immersed in a holy river or the sea. Śrāddha ceremonies are followed by सपिण्डीकरण (affiliation of the dead with the manes).

antaryāmin
(‘One who controls from within’)
------------------------------------------
According to the उपनिषद्स्, ब्रह्मन् is both the immanent and the transcendent Reality. Having created the world, ब्रह्मन् enters into it (vide Taittirīyopaniṣad 2.6) and controls it from within (vide Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad 3.7.3-23). In this aspect it is called the ‘antaryāmin,’ the inner controller.
In Advaita Vedānta, the individual self is ultimately identical with the antar-yāmin. But in द्वैत and Viśiṣṭādvaita, the two are different.
In the Pāñcarātra school of Vaiṣṇa-vism, God manifests himself in four forms retaining the पर or the highest form in his world called वैकुण्ठ: vyūha (the four emanations), विभव (incarnations), arca (manifestation through the image during worship) and अन्तर्यामिन् (the inner controller). According to this school, the last is only a partial manifestation.

antaḥkaraṇa
(‘the inner instrument’)
------------------------------------------
The general name by which मिन्द् is known in the Hindu scriptural works is ‘antaḥkaraṇa,’ the ‘inner (antaḥ) instrument (karaṇa).’ Even though the external sense-organs like the eye or the ear are functioning, no चोग्नितिओन् becomes possible unless the मिन्द् is connected with them. Hence the significance of the name.
Among the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् viz., जाग्रत् (waking state), स्वप्न (dream state) and सुषुप्ति (deep sleep state), the अन्तःकरण is actively functioning in the first two and dormant in the third.
This अन्तःकरण functions in four different ways and gets four different names according to the functions. While functioning as the receptive and retentive faculty it is called ‘citta’ or मिन्द्-stuff; as the questioning, doubting and willing faculty, it is called ‘manas’ or मिन्द्; as the deciding faculty it is called ‘buddhi’ or intelligence; and as the identifying faculty which identifies itself with each of these functions it is called ‘ahaṅkāra’ or the ego.
These words are sometimes used to mean the अन्तःकरण or मिन्द् as a whole and sometimes to mean the particular faculty indicated. The sense in which they are used has to be made out from the context.
See also AHAṄKĀRA, BUDDHI, CITTA, MANAS and MIND.

Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad which forms an important part of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa of the Śukla Yajurveda is by far the biggest of the extant उपनिषद्स्. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa is found to be in two शाखास् or recensions, the Kāṇva and the Mādhyandina. Hence the Upaniṣad also is found to have two recensions.
The seventh section—each such section is known as a ‘brāhmaṇa’—of the third chapter of this Upaniṣad is called Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa since it deals with the topic of ब्रह्मन् as the अन्तर्यामिन् (‘the indwelling spirit’).
The third chapter starts with the convening of a conference of ‘knowers of ब्रह्मन्’ by the king जनक of Videha, who expresses a desire to know the best among them (brahmiṣṭha), and offers rich presents. The sage याज्ञवल्क्य comes forward to take away the presents even before proving his mettle in the assembly. This naturally enrages the assembled sages who start challenging him with intricate philosophical queries. However, याज्ञवल्क्य proves more than a match for all of them.
The seventh brāhmaṇa—which is the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa—starts with the question of उद्दालक आरुणि about the अन्तर्यामिन् or the indwelling spirit in the universe. याज्ञवल्क्य replies that it is the आत्मन् or the Self that resides in everything, whether it is the elements like the earth, or the worlds like हेअवेन् or living beings or sense organs or मिन्द्, and controls them all from within. He knows them but they know him not. He is actually the knower and can never become an object of perception or knowledge. He is the eternal Self of all.
If the Kāṇvaśākhā stops with this, the Mādhyandinaśakhā continues the description and adds ‘ya ātmani tiṣṭhan...’ (‘who, remaining inside the आत्मन्...’) which lends strength to the belief that the आत्मन् (the individual self) and ब्रह्मन् (the Supreme Self) are different and that the latter controls the former. This comes in handy for the dualistic schools like Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta to defend their position.

antyaja
(‘the last-born’)
------------------------------------------
Division of society based on the nature and nurture of the individuals as also their professions is a phenomenon found in many parts of the civilized world. In the special context of India’s ancient history when races and cultures battled and blended, this division also took a unique shape. This is known as the ‘jātipaddhati’ or चस्ते स्य्स्तेम्. जाति also means birth. Since children usually adopted the professions of their fathers and forefathers, caste came to acquire a functional character in a self-contained economy and a social structure, based on traditional values.
The वर्ण system from which caste is supposed to have originated was a simple division based on गुण (natural characteristics) and कर्म (action, acts, vocation). This gradually developed into a labyrinth of jātis and upajātis or castes and sub-castes most of which were grouped under an umbrella term called the ‘śūdras.’ Even among such castes, a few were pushed to the lowest rung of the social ladder because of their unclean ड़ोओद् habits and amoral attitude which were unacceptable to the rest of society. Hence the name ‘antyaja’ (‘the last-born’). Probably for the same reason they were also considered aspṛśyas or untouchables. However, neither in the वेदस् nor in the earlier smṛtis and धर्मशास्त्रस् have they been treated as such, but only as शूद्रस्. The practice of untouchability seems to be a post-Vedic phenomenon.
Some of the castes branded as antyajas are: caṇḍāla, rajaka (the washerman), carmakāra (worker in hides), buruḍa (bamboo worker), kaivarta (the fisherman) and bhilla (of a forest-tribe or a hill-tribe).
During the medieval ages, these castes had often risen in social status due to their organization and wealth.
Though caste barriers have existed in some form all along at social levels, birth in a low caste has never been considered a bar to spiritual enlightenment as depicted in the story of धर्मव्याध (vide Mahābharata, Vanaparva, 210). Indian history is replete with stories of great saints, who, though born as antyajas, rose to very high spiritual states and were recognized and respected as such by the society. To mention only a few: कण्णप्प, रैदास्, Cokkameḷa, नन्दनार् and Tiruppāṇi.
Eradication of untouchability which is a social curse, has been attempted by several religious and social leaders in India throughout the centuries. The success, however, has not been proportionate to the efforts put forth. Economic, educational and cultural upliftment of the masses is the only solution to this social malady. Since independence the Indian Constitution has positively forbidden the observance, in any form, of untouchability and these socially disabled communities are being given special consideration in matters of एदुचतिओन् and employment, and, many economic benefits.
See also ASPṚŚYATĀ.

antarāla
(‘that which exists in between’)
------------------------------------------
Temples or houses of God, have been in existence since a long time. The earliest of the हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस् as we see them today might have been built during the third or fourth centuries A. D. The most important part of the Hindu temple is the sanctum sanctorum known as गर्भगृह, the ‘womb होउसे,’ housing the image of the deity. अन्तराल is the narrow passage that connects this गर्भगृह to the large hall or pavilion, called maṇṭapa which is normally used for congregational religious acts. This अन्तराल is also called ardha-maṇṭapa or शुकनासी.
In temple symbology, the अन्तराल represents the neck of the deity, if the whole temple complex represents the body of the deity.
